article_title: Generalizing a Highly Configurable Analytics Pipeline to Replicate and Support Educational Research Across Multiple Domains
citation: Y. Bai, P. Thajchayapong, A. Goel. (2025). Generalizing a Highly Configurable Analytics Pipeline to Replicate and Support Educational Research Across Multiple Domains. https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.11877
title: Highly Configurable System design for cross-domain learning analytics
description: The pipeline applies Highly Configurable System (HCS) principles, "enabling a single underlying codebase to be applied to different scenarios through flexible configuration". Each statistical option's parameters — alternative hypothesis, dataset, independent and dependent variables, and result storage location — are programmed as variables whose values are read from keys in the JSON analysis configuration payload, so the same analysis-module code serves different domains. Santana et al 2025 found this yields a pipeline that is extensible and flexible while maintaining structural coherence, defined as the absence of invalid system configurations.
requirements: Analysis configuration payloads must supply valid values for each configurable key (statistic name, dataset, variables, result file name).
constraints: Structural coherence depends on configurations being valid; the balance between flexibility and structural coherence was established in prior work by Santana et al 2025.
target_learners: researchers and instructors analyzing educational AI assistant data
target_learning_goals: reproducible cross-domain analysis of learner interaction data
examples: Table 1 shows differing payload key values for JW, VERA, and SAMI Welch's t-tests feeding the same underlying analysis code.
key_sources: Y. Bai, P. Thajchayapong, A. Goel. (2025). Generalizing a Highly Configurable Analytics Pipeline to Replicate and Support Educational Research Across Multiple Domains. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.30303

article_title: Competency gaps in emergency obstetric and neonatal care: Assessing knowledge, skills, and confidence in the use of magnesium sulfate among providers in Malawi.
citation: Kamanga Martha, Kapalamula Felister, Kazembe Abigail, Kabondo Charity, Chakhame Bertha, Lungu Gaily, Kumbani Lilly, Chodzaza Elizabeth. (2026). Competency gaps in emergency obstetric and neonatal care: Assessing knowledge, skills, and confidence in the use of magnesium sulfate among providers in Malawi. Women's Health. https://doi.org/10.1177/17455057261471323
title: Human-Centred Design as a participatory approach for identifying competency barriers and co-creating solutions in maternal health
description: The article describes HCD as "a participatory approach that values empathy, creativity, and collaboration with end-users when designing practical, contextually appropriate interventions." Techniques included journey mapping, systems mapping, ranking exercises, and low-fidelity prototyping, which surfaced hidden barriers such as workflow inefficiencies, cognitive overload, and emotional stress. The approach enabled providers to move beyond identifying challenges to developing solutions enhancing clinical practice and health system responsiveness.
requirements: Engagement of end-users (providers) in participatory techniques such as journey mapping and prototyping
constraints: Applied in low-resource maternity settings in Malawi; the article notes past research shows HCD innovations are more acceptable, feasible, and sustainable in such contexts
target_learning_goals: identifying barriers to emergency obstetric care
co-designing clinical decision-support and training interventions
examples: Eight one-day HCD workshops with 48 participants generated co-created solutions including laminated dosage charts and peer-led simulations
key_sources: Kamanga Martha, Kapalamula Felister, Kazembe Abigail, Kabondo Charity, Chakhame Bertha, Lungu Gaily, Kumbani Lilly, Chodzaza Elizabeth. (2026). Competency gaps in emergency obstetric and neonatal care: Assessing knowledge, skills, and confidence in the use of magnesium sulfate among providers in Malawi. Women's Health. https://doi.org/10.1177/17455057261471323

article_title: Unlocking minds: fostering critical thinking in postgraduates trainees through a foundation course - a prospective quasi-experimental study.
citation: Singh Veena Kumari, Singh Shruti, Tiwari Meenakshi, Haq Ansarul, Sharma Sarsij, Moudgil Tania. (2025). Unlocking minds: fostering critical thinking in postgraduates trainees through a foundation course - a prospective quasi-experimental study. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-07355-9
title: Holistic Critical Thinking Scoring Rubric (HCTSR) used to assess quality of critical thinking in written and verbal postgraduate work
description: The HCTSR is "a rating measure to assess the quality of critical thinking displayed in a verbal presentation or written text in any educational program or assessment process." The article notes it requires a task where "the thinker is asked to explain their thinking process and not just to provide the conclusions," that its criteria help learners internalize characteristics of strong and weak critical thinking, and that it has demonstrated strong inter-rater reliability and construct validity across diverse educational settings. Two trained faculty raters scored essays and case-scenario presentations on a 1-4 scale, resolving discrepancies by consensus.
requirements: Raters must be trained and strong enough to make accurate judgments, since "The ratings on this scale will only be as valid as the strength of the raters"
constraints: No assessment tool is universally superior in all contexts, per the article; pre-course HCTSR baselines were not collected in this study
target_learning_goals: Assessing quality of critical thinking in written and verbal performance
examples: Applied to a common-topic essay and a real-life case-scenario verbal presentation; scores averaged; 4 = strong, 3 = acceptable, 2 = unacceptable, 1 = significantly weak critical thinker
key_sources: Singh Veena Kumari, Singh Shruti, Tiwari Meenakshi, Haq Ansarul, Sharma Sarsij, Moudgil Tania. (2025). Unlocking minds: fostering critical thinking in postgraduates trainees through a foundation course - a prospective quasi-experimental study. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-07355-9

article_title: Design and evaluation of children's education interactive learning system based on human computer interaction technology.
citation: Li Mengru, Lv Yang, Pu Yongming, Wu Min. (2025). Design and evaluation of children’s education interactive learning system based on human computer interaction technology. Scientific Reports 15, 6135. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-025-90800-y
title: Layered HCI interactive learning system for children's education with VR/AR content
description: An interactive learning system for children in grades 1–6 that integrates multimedia technologies including VR and AR to create a dynamic learning environment. Its architecture comprises a user interface layer, an interactive logic layer, a content management layer, a data management layer and a database system; the article states the user interface layer encompasses "all front-end elements, such as buttons, pictures, videos, and interactive games". Educational content is stratified by children's age and learning ability.
requirements: Event-driven interaction logic with real-time response to user inputs
Multi-level database architecture for user information, learning progress and interactive data
Age-stratified educational content tailored to cognitive level
constraints: Evaluated primarily in a single educational institution
Performance assessed under controlled conditions; real-world environments may vary due to network instability or differing hardware
examples: The experimental group used the system while a control group followed traditional teaching methods, with 100 participants randomly assigned and stratified by age, grade and gender.
key_sources: Li Mengru, Lv Yang, Pu Yongming, Wu Min. (2025). Design and evaluation of children’s education interactive learning system based on human computer interaction technology. Scientific Reports 15, 6135. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-025-90800-y

article_title: Human-Centered Design in Graduate Nursing Education: Outcomes From a Cohort Study.
citation: Holt JM, Talsma A, Lloren JIC, Eljarrah I, Woehrle L, Avdeev I. (2025). Human-Centered Design in Graduate Nursing Education: Outcomes From a Cohort Study. Nurse Educator. https://doi.org/10.1097/NNE.0000000000001778
title: Human-centered design as an iterative, user-as-expert methodology distinguished from broader design thinking
description: The article defines human-centered design (HCD) as "a methodology that focuses on understanding a problem from users' (eg, patients, families, nurses) point-of-view and developing an innovative strategy or creative solution to address it." HCD iteratively "tests and validates the solution through iterations of prototyping that engage stakeholders," producing user-driven innovations in practices, policies, and technology. It is distinguished from design thinking, described as a broader five-step methodology (empathizing, defining, ideating, prototyping, testing) whose goal "may or may not be user-focused." In HCD, unlike the traditional linear approach to health intervention research, "the users are the experts, and innovation emerges from several cycles of empathy, ideation, prototyping, and testing."
requirements: Solutions must be developed through iterative prototyping cycles that engage stakeholders and start from users' point-of-view
constraints: The article frames HCD within health care and nursing innovation contexts; design thinking, in contrast, can be applied across disciplines
target_learning_goals: developing user-driven solutions to health care problems and changing systems, processes, or products
examples: Participants endorsed seeking feedback, integrative thinking, optimism, and experimentalism after the I&HCD workshop
key_sources: Holt JM, Talsma A, Lloren JIC, Eljarrah I, Woehrle L, Avdeev I. (2025). Human-Centered Design in Graduate Nursing Education: Outcomes From a Cohort Study. Nurse Educator. https://doi.org/10.1097/NNE.0000000000001778

article_title: Skills for generalist and specialist nurses working in the prevention and control of infections in Brazil.
citation: Massaroli Aline, Martini Jussara Gue, Moya José Luis Medina, Pereira Milca Severino, Tipple Anaclara Ferreira Veiga, Maestri Eleine. (2019). Skills for generalist and specialist nurses working in the prevention and control of infections in Brazil. Revista Latino-Americana de Enfermagem. https://doi.org/10.1590/1518-8345.2620.3134
title: Consensual list of 35 named and described HCRI competencies for generalist and specialist nurses (Tables 1-3)
description: The study's central artifact is a list of competencies with name and description, organized in three tables: 4 core competencies (Table 1), 14 generic competencies for the generalist nurse (Table 2) and 17 specific competencies for the specialist nurse (Table 3), each with its coefficient of variation. The article reports that "the competences were organized in 4 core, 14 generic and 17 specific, with name and description of each competency". Descriptions detail what each competency involves, e.g. hand hygiene "involves the knowledge about microorganisms of the hands, contaminating microorganisms, understanding the importance of HH, mastering the techniques".
requirements: Each competency is documented with a name and a description so it can guide teaching
constraints: Specific competencies reuse dimensions of the generic competencies, adding specialist-level depth rather than replacing them
target_learning_goals: prevention and control of healthcare-related infections
examples: Generic competencies include hand hygiene, use of Personal Protective Equipment, maintenance of aseptic chain and health services waste management
key_sources: Massaroli Aline, Martini Jussara Gue, Moya José Luis Medina, Pereira Milca Severino, Tipple Anaclara Ferreira Veiga, Maestri Eleine. (2019). Skills for generalist and specialist nurses working in the prevention and control of infections in Brazil. Revista Latino-Americana de Enfermagem. https://doi.org/10.1590/1518-8345.2620.3134
